## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">Does class background change how AI use is judged?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 10 considered how people interpret AI-assisted messages between friends and colleagues. This week turns to a report at work. Two writers with the same job and the same report may be judged differently if readers know about their family backgrounds or their use of AI. We use the assigned studies to design that comparison.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of class, you should be able to:

- explain the AI-use evaluation penalty identified by Reif and colleagues and describe the outcome they measured;
- describe Foschi’s account of status-based standards for competence;
- explain how Rafalow’s schools assigned different value to similar digital practices;
- distinguish competence, laziness, trust and the perceived legitimacy of AI assistance;
- use a nested Python loop to prepare four versions of one report, varying family background and AI disclosure.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Status and competence:** Martha Foschi (2000), “Double Standards for Competence: Theory and Research,” *Annual Review of Sociology* 26: 21–42. A review of research on how status can change the evidence observers require before judging someone competent. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.soc.26.1.21). [@Foschi2000DoubleStandards]
- **Judging AI users:** Jessica A. Reif, Richard P. Larrick and Jack B. Soll (2025), “Evidence of a Social Evaluation Penalty for Using Artificial Intelligence,” *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* 122: e2426766122. Experiments in which observers rate workers who use AI, receive human help or work without described help. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2426766122). [@ReifLarrickSoll2025]
- **Digital skill in schools:** Matthew H. Rafalow (2018), “Disciplining Play: Digital Youth Culture as Capital at School,” *American Journal of Sociology* 123(5): 1416–1452. Ethnographic evidence that teachers in three schools attached different educational value to students’ digital practices. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/695766). [@Rafalow2018DiscipliningPlay]
- **Disclosure and trust:** Oliver Schilke and Martin Reimann (2025), “The Transparency Dilemma: How AI Disclosure Erodes Trust,” *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes* 188: 104405. Experiments on trust in people who disclose AI assistance; Study 11 concerns a monthly competitor report. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104405). [@SchilkeReimann2025Transparency]
:::

## Sociological and methodological background

Foschi reviews studies in which observers apply different standards of competence to people with different social statuses. The same performance can carry different evidentiary weight depending on who produced it. For our proposed study, family background might change whether AI use is read as resourceful or as a sign of weak skill. The pretest will ask what readers infer from the family-background descriptions. [@Foschi2000DoubleStandards]

Bourdieu’s linguistic market asks how speech and writing acquire value in a particular setting and why speakers enter that setting with different authority. He criticized accounts of linguistic competence that stop at the capacity to produce grammatical sentences. A model can now supply Alex with sentences he did not compose. Alex still decides whether to use them in this report, and a manager may judge that decision. Lamont and Lareau press us to identify which signals an institution recognizes as valuable. [@Bourdieu1977Linguistic; @LamontLareau1988CulturalCapital]

Rafalow observed three schools in which teachers assigned different value to students’ digital practices. At affluent Heathcliff, a teacher brought a student’s periodic-table game into a lesson. At working-class César Chávez, a teacher acknowledged students’ gaming abilities but emphasized keyboarding, research and written assignments. His fieldnotes show teachers deciding which digital practices count as educational skill. [@Rafalow2018DiscipliningPlay]

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Reif, Larrick and Soll ran four preregistered experiments on how people judge AI users. In Study 2, workers described as using AI were rated lazier than workers receiving comparable human help or no described help; they were also rated lower on competence and related traits. Study 3 showed that evaluators’ own AI use mattered when they judged an AI-using applicant. These results lead us to ask how an evaluator’s reading of AI use might change with information about a worker’s background. [@ReifLarrickSoll2025]

Schilke and Reimann study trust in people who disclose AI assistance. In Study 11, participants played a head of marketing evaluating a market research analyst’s monthly competitor report. Prior information about the analyst’s use of AI tools and a statement with the report that GrowthBar had been used were varied separately. Mean trust was 4.10 with disclosure and 4.62 without it, on a 1–7 scale. The control report left AI use unmentioned. Our proposed study measures trust and competence separately. [@SchilkeReimann2025Transparency]

Our proposed experiment keeps Alex Harper’s job, degree, three years of experience and fictional competitor report identical. It varies a family-background description and whether Alex discloses using ChatGPT to edit the wording. Human readers could rate competence, trust, report quality and the acceptability of assistance. The Python exercise prepares the four descriptions. A pretest asks what readers infer from the descriptions of parental education and work.

## Reading discussion

1. What exactly do Reif’s participants evaluate? How is that different from judging the quality of the work itself?
2. Foschi allows more than one prediction about workers from different class backgrounds. Which expectations would produce each result?
3. What did the teachers in Rafalow’s fieldnotes recognize as useful digital skill? How did their practices differ across schools?
4. Why might the AI disclosure in Schilke and Reimann’s competitor-report study lower trust? Would that necessarily imply lower perceived competence?
5. How would you check that readers interpret the background descriptions as intended?

## In-class Python walkthrough

Use the fictional report to request one careful model edit. Check the raw response against the stated facts, including the absence of customer-switching data. Then use a nested loop to place the same revised report in four descriptions varying family background and AI disclosure. Trace the first two passes and discuss the questions you would ask human readers.

This is an in-class walkthrough and optional practice. **No Week 11 video is due. No reading, coding or other work is assigned for the cancelled class on 25 November.**

## Summary and preparation

The existing experiments document penalties in how AI users are judged. Bourdieu, Foschi and Rafalow help us ask whether readers value the same AI use differently when they know a worker’s family background. The proposed four-condition study would test the size and direction of that difference.
